meaning: Quotes written text: 「〜と書いてある」 means “it says ... (on it)”, and 「〜と読む」 means “it is read as ...”.
connection: Quoted content + と (casual: って) + 書いてある／読む

senses.label: It says ...
senses.meaning: Reports what is written on a sign, a manual, a letter, and so on, like “it says ...”. It simply states that the words are there; who wrote them doesn't matter.
senses.connection: Quoted content + と書いてある／と書いてあります (in writing also 「〜と書かれている」); often with 「ここに」, 「看板に」, 「メールに」
examples: The sign says “No Entry”.
The email said tomorrow is a day off.
What does this paper say?

senses.label: It's read as ...
senses.meaning: Explains how a kanji or word is read, like “it's read ...” or “it's pronounced ...”. To ask for a reading, say 「何と読みますか」.
senses.connection: Reading + と読む／と読みます; question: 何と読みますか
examples: This kanji is read 「やま」.
「明日」 can also be read 「あした」.
Excuse me, how do you read this?

notes: For a reading, use 「と」, never 「を」, or the meaning changes to “read (a text)”: ✕「この漢字は『やま』を読みます」→ ○「この漢字は『やま』と読みます」. 「本を読む」 is reading a book; 「やまと読む」 is “read as やま”.
When you only say “a name / some words are written” without quoting the actual content, use 「が」: ○「ここに名前が書いてある」. ✕「ここに名前と書いてある」 would be understood as the paper literally saying the word “名前”.
When the paper or sign is the topic (“it says on it”), use 「書いてある」. 「書いている」 means “someone is writing”: ✕「看板に『禁止』と書いている」→ ○「看板に『禁止』と書いてある」.
When reporting a document's content to a boss or client, say 「〜と書いてあります」 or 「〜と記載されています」. 「〜って書いてある」 is casual talk between friends and sounds careless in a report.

daily.title: Reading a notice at the station
daily.description: Looking at a station notice with a friend and reporting what it says.
daily.example: It says the trains are stopped until ten.

daily.title: Asking how to read a kanji
daily.description: Asking a Japanese friend about a character you can't read.
daily.example: How do you read this character?

daily.title: Reading medicine instructions
daily.description: A family member reminds you how to take your medicine.
daily.example: It says to take it three times a day.

work.title: Checking a contract clause
work.description: Reporting a rule in a document to your boss.
work.example: The contract says payment is due by the end of the month.

work.title: Checking how a client's name is read
work.description: Before meeting a client, checking with a coworker how to say their name.

etymology: 「書く」 originally meant “to scratch, to carve”, and later came to mean “to write”. 「〜てある」 shows the state left by an action. 「読む」 originally meant “to count, to read out one by one”, and later “to read; to read as”. 「と」 is the quotation particle.
formation: Made of the quoting particle 「と」 + the te-form of 「書く」 + 「ある」. 「と」 works like quotation marks, wrapping the content before it as a block: “in the form of these words”. 「〜てある」 shows that someone did an action and its result has stayed in place. Together they mean “has been written as … and left there”, so the focus is on the words left behind, not on the writer, and the writer usually isn't mentioned. In 「と読む」, 「と」 likewise wraps a sound: “read with the sound …”. With 「を」, the object is the thing being read (a book, a newspaper); with 「と」, it is the sound you produce. That is why 「本を読む」 and 「やまと読む」 mean different things.

similar.title: 〜てある
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「書いてある」 is simply 「〜てある」 applied to 「書く」, the state of someone having written something that stays there. 「〜てある」 works with all kinds of transitive verbs (「窓が開けてある」); this pattern is specifically for quoting written words.

similar.title: 〜と言う (quotation)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both quote content with 「と」. 「〜と言う」 quotes words someone said out loud, and the subject is the speaker; 「〜と書いてある」 quotes words on paper, the subject is the place where they are written, and who wrote them doesn't matter.

similar.title: 〜によると・〜によれば
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both can tell where information comes from. 「天気予報によると明日は雨だそうだ」 names the source and often ends with 「そうだ」; 「ここに明日は雨だと書いてある」 directly relays the words in front of you.

similar.title: 〜という意味だ
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: often used together with this pattern. 「何と書いてありますか」 asks what the words say; 「どういう意味ですか」 asks what they mean. First you read the words, then you explain the meaning.

meaning: Reports what someone said, like “(someone) said ...”. Often used to pass on a message.
connection: Plain-form sentence + と (casual: って) + 言っていた／言っていました (casual: 言ってた)

senses.label: Passing on a message
senses.meaning: Tells the listener what a third person said, like “X said ...”. Using 「言っていた」 instead of 「言った」 shows that what was said still holds now.
senses.connection: Person + が／は + plain form + と言っていた／と言っていました; casual: って言ってた
examples: Mr. Tanaka said he can't come tomorrow.
The teacher said the test won't be hard.
Mom said to come home early.

senses.label: Keeps saying
senses.meaning: 「〜と言っている」 means someone says this now, or has been saying it for a while. Often used with 「いつも」 or 「ずっと」, and in the news to report what an organization says.
senses.connection: Person + は + plain form + と言っている／と言っています
examples: My little brother always says he wants to be a doctor.
My father says he'll quit his job next year.

notes: When passing on your own boss's words to a client or another company, don't use honorifics: ✕「部長が〜とおっしゃっていました」→ ○「部長の田中が〜と申しておりました」. Use 「おっしゃっていました」 only for words from the other side (a client, a teacher, etc.).
「〜って言ってた」 is casual speech between friends. When passing a message to your boss, say 「〜と言っていました」 or 「〜とおっしゃっていました」; 「って言ってた」 sounds offhand and disrespectful.
In indirect reporting, use the plain form before 「と」: ✕「田中さんは明日来ますと言っていた」→ ○「田中さんは明日来ると言っていた」. To keep the original です/ます style, quote it directly in 「」.
To relay a request or order, use 「〜てほしいと言っていた」 or 「〜ようにと言っていた」. Dropping in 「来い」 or 「来て」 as is makes the original sound rude, or sounds like you are ordering the listener yourself.

daily.title: Passing on a message to family
daily.description: After a friend calls, telling your family what they said.
daily.example: Ken said he'll call later.

daily.title: Chatting with a classmate
daily.description: Reporting what the teacher said in class.
daily.example: The teacher said there's a test next week.

work.title: Passing on a client's request to your boss
work.description: Telling your boss what a client said.
work.example: Mr. Yamamoto said he'd like the delivery date pushed back a week.

work.title: Leaving a message for a coworker
work.description: Passing on a message to a coworker who was away from their desk.
work.example: The department manager said to please come to the meeting room at three.

etymology: 「言う」 means “to say”, and 「〜ていた」 is the past of the continuous 「〜ている」. Using the continuous form treats “having said it” as a state that still holds, which suits passing on messages.
formation: Made of the quoting particle 「と」 + the te-form of 「言う」 + 「いた」, the past of 「いる」. 「と」 wraps what the other person said; 「言っている」 here doesn't mean “is saying right now” but treats “there is such a statement” as an existing state. Putting it in the past 「いた」 means that at that point in the past, the person held that statement. While plain 「言った」 only reports the act of saying, 「言っていた」 puts the weight on the information “that's what they said”, which is why it is perfect for passing on messages. The present 「言っている」 means the person still claims it now.

similar.title: 〜と言う (quotation)
similar.explanation: Same origin: this pattern is the 「ていた」 form of 「と言う」. 「田中さんは来ないと言った」 just narrates the act of saying; 「田中さんは来ないと言っていた」 passes the statement on to the listener as information, which sounds more natural when relaying a message.

similar.title: 〜と聞いた
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both relay news you heard. 「〜と聞いた」 has “I” as the subject (“I heard”); 「〜と言っていた」 has the person who said it as the subject, so the source is clearer.

similar.title: 〜そうだ (hearsay)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both report what others said. 「〜そうだ」 just means “apparently”, often without saying who said it, and follows the plain form; 「〜と言っていた」 usually names the specific person.

similar.title: 〜んだって
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜んだって」 is a very colloquial way to pass on news, “I heard that …, you know”; 「〜と言っていた」 is more neutral, works in polite style as 「〜と言っていました」, and can be used when relaying a message to your boss.

meaning: Shows that a thought or opinion continues over time. Also used to describe what a third person thinks.
connection: Plain-form sentence + と思っている (casual: と思ってる)

senses.label: Have been thinking
senses.meaning: The thought isn't momentary; you have felt this way for some time, like “I've always thought ...”. It stresses continuity more than 「〜と思う」.
senses.connection: Plain form + と思っている／と思っています; often with 「ずっと」 or 「前から」
examples: I've always wanted to study abroad in Japan.
I feel this job suits me.

senses.label: What others think
senses.meaning: To describe someone else's thoughts, use 「〜と思っている」. You can't simply say 「彼は〜と思う」. Like “he thinks ...”.
senses.connection: Third person + は + plain form + と思っている
examples: My mother thinks I'm still a child.
Everyone thought he was the culprit.
My older sister thinks she's the prettiest.

senses.label: Thought (wrongly)
senses.meaning: The past 「〜と思っていた」 means you used to think something, but now you know it's not so, like “I thought ...”.
senses.connection: Plain form + と思っていた; often followed by 「のに」 or 「けど」
examples: I thought today was a day off, but there was class.
I thought it would be easier.

notes: For someone else's opinion you must use 「〜と思っている」: ✕「田中さんは無理だと思う」 is understood as “(I) think Tanaka can't do it” → ○「田中さんは無理だと思っている」 (Tanaka thinks it's impossible).
What comes before changes the meaning completely: with the volitional form, 「行こうと思っている」 means “I'm planning to go”; with the plain form, 「行くと思っている」 means “thinks (someone) will go”.
「〜と思っていました」 often implies “I had assumed …, but it wasn't so”. Saying 「もっと安いと思っていました」 to a client sounds like a complaint about the price; to express an expectation, 「〜と期待していました」 is safer.

When giving an opinion on the spot, 「〜と思います」 is enough. Answering your boss's “What do you think?” with 「〜と思っています」 sounds like your mind was made up long ago and isn't open to discussion, which comes across as strong.

daily.title: Talking about your dream
daily.description: Telling a friend about a long-term dream.
daily.example: I've always wanted to have my own shop someday.

daily.title: Complaining about family
daily.description: Grumbling to a friend about your parents' views.
daily.example: My dad thinks video games are bad.

daily.title: Realizing a mistake
daily.description: Arriving at a shop and finding it closed.
daily.example: I thought it was open today.

work.title: Stating goals in an interview
work.description: Explaining a long-held wish to the interviewer.
work.example: I have long wanted to work at your company.

work.title: Analyzing a client's view
work.description: Explaining a client's opinion in a meeting.
work.example: The client seems to think the price is too high.

etymology: 「思う」 basically means “to think in one's heart”. 「〜ている」 shows a continuing state. Together they present a thought as an ongoing state, so they can describe others' thoughts objectively.
formation: Made of the quoting particle 「と」 + the te-form of 「思う」 + 「いる」. 「と」 wraps the content of the thought. 「思う」 on its own is a judgment formed in the mind at the moment of speaking, and only the speaker knows it, so plain 「と思う」 can only mean “I think”. Adding 「ている」, which shows a continuing state, turns the judgment into a lasting mental state that can be described from the outside like a fact. So it can be used for a third person, and can also mean “have always thought so”. The past form 「と思っていた」 shows a thought held in the past, and often implies that it later turned out not to be true: “I had assumed”.

similar.title: 〜と思う (I think)
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜と思う」 is a judgment the speaker makes on the spot and is used only in the first person. Adding 「ている」 turns it into an ongoing thought, which can describe a third person or mean “have always thought so”.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うと思う
similar.explanation: Same origin: with the volitional form before it, it means “intend to”: 「来年留学しようと思っている」 is a plan you have had for a while. With the plain form, it's an opinion: 「彼は来ると思っている」.

similar.title: 〜だろうと思う
similar.explanation: Same origin: adding 「だろう」 before 「思う」 makes the judgment a guess with some uncertainty; 「〜と思っている」 focuses on the thought continuing to exist and doesn't express a degree of guessing.

similar.title: 〜がる・〜がっている
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both describe a third person's inner state. 「〜がっている」 describes feelings or wishes visible from the outside (「行きたがっている」); 「〜と思っている」 describes inner opinions and judgments.

meaning: Embeds a yes-no question in a sentence as an object or topic, like “whether (or not) ...”.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form, or na-adjective stem / noun + かどうか

senses.label: Whether (as object)
senses.meaning: Puts a yes-no question inside a sentence, followed by 「分からない」, 「聞く」, 「確かめる」, 「調べる」, and so on. Like “whether ...” or “if ...”.
senses.connection: Plain form (no 「だ」 after na-adjectives and nouns) + かどうか + 分かる／知る／聞く／確かめる
examples: I don't know whether it will rain tomorrow.
I'll ask him if he's coming.
Please check whether that story is true.

senses.label: Whether (as topic)
senses.meaning: Followed by 「は」 or 「が」, “whether ...” becomes the topic or subject. Common as 「〜かどうかは〜次第だ」 or 「〜かどうかが問題だ」.
senses.connection: Plain form + かどうかは／かどうかが + predicate
examples: I haven't decided yet whether to go.
Whether it tastes good is what matters most.

notes: After nouns and na-adjectives, don't add 「だ」: ✕「本当だかどうか」→ ○「本当かどうか」.
If the clause contains a question word (何・どこ・いつ, etc.), don't use 「かどうか」: ✕「何時に来るかどうか分からない」→ ○「何時に来るか分からない」.
「かどうか」 can't stand alone as a question: ✕「明日来るかどうか？」→ ○「明日来る？」. To ask someone, say 「来られるかどうか、教えていただけますか」.
Answering a client with just 「参加するかどうか分かりません」 sounds cold and irresponsible. In business, say 「参加できるかどうか、確認してご連絡いたします」.

daily.title: Checking before meeting friends
daily.description: Planning a weekend trip but unsure about the weather.
daily.example: I'm worried whether it'll be sunny.

daily.title: Before shopping online
daily.description: Talking with family about clothing sizes.
daily.example: I don't know if the size will fit.

work.title: Checking the other side's schedule
work.example: I'll confirm whether next week works for them.

work.title: Discussing whether a project is feasible
work.description: Discussing in a meeting whether the plan can work.
work.example: The question is whether we can do it within budget.

etymology: It is made of the question particle 「か」 + the question word 「どう」 (how) + 「か」. Originally “is it ..., or how is it?”, it became a set phrase for “whether”.
formation: Made of the question particle 「か」 + the question adverb 「どう」 (“how”) + 「か」. The first 「か」 turns the content before it into the question “is it …?”. 「どうか」 originally means “or how (else)”, standing for the other possibility, “not so”. Together they mean “is it …, or otherwise?”, laying out both options, yes and no, which gives the meaning “whether or not”. Because it already contains both options, it can't be combined with question words like 何 or どこ. You can also spell out both options as 「〜か〜ないか」 with the same meaning.

similar.title: 〜か (embedded question)
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use 「か」 to embed a question in a sentence. With a question word, use 「〜か」 (「誰が来るか分からない」); without one, when asking “whether or not”, use 「〜かどうか」 (「彼が来るかどうか分からない」).

similar.title: 〜か否か
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜か否か」 means the same as 「〜かどうか」 but is written language, used mostly in papers, news and formal documents. In everyday conversation people say 「かどうか」.

meaning: A casual sentence ending for wondering to yourself, hoping for something, or softly asking the listener.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form, or na-adjective stem / noun (+ なの) + かな (drawn out: かなあ)

senses.label: Wondering
senses.meaning: The speaker isn't sure and wonders aloud, like “I wonder ...”. No answer is expected, and the tone is light.
senses.connection: Plain form + かな; often with 「本当に」, 「大丈夫」, 「〜のかな」
examples: I wonder if it'll be sunny tomorrow.
I wonder if this is really OK.
I wonder if he's home yet.

senses.label: Hoping
senses.meaning: 「〜ないかな」 shows you hope something happens, like “I wish ...” or “Why isn't it ... yet?”.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + かな (なあ); often with 「早く」
examples: I wish summer vacation would hurry up and come.
I wish someone would help me.

senses.label: Soft request
senses.meaning: Asks or requests something softly from someone close, leaving room to say no, like “Is it OK if ...?”. To a superior, use 「〜でしょうか」 instead.
senses.connection: 〜てもいいかな／〜てくれるかな／〜てもらえるかな
examples: Can I talk to you for a minute?
Could you carry this bag for me?

notes: Saying 「〜てもらえるかな」 to a boss or client is how a superior talks to a subordinate and sounds very rude. To superiors, say 「〜ていただけないでしょうか」.
「〜ないかな」 usually expresses a wish, not a negative guess: 「早く夏休みにならないかな」 means “I wish summer vacation would come soon”, not “maybe there won't be a vacation”.

「かな」 shows you're not sure, while 「だろう」 shows you're fairly confident: 「明日は晴れるかな」 (will it be sunny?) / 「明日は晴れるだろう」 (it'll probably be sunny). In formal situations, switch to 「〜でしょうか」 and 「〜でしょう」 respectively.
After nouns and na-adjectives, don't add 「だ」: ✕「誰だかな」→ ○「誰かな」, 「大丈夫かな」.

daily.title: Checking the sky before going out
daily.description: Looking at a cloudy sky and talking to yourself.
daily.example: Maybe I should take an umbrella.

daily.title: Waiting for a friend
daily.description: Your friend is late and you mutter to yourself.
daily.example: Not here yet? They're so late.

daily.title: Asking a friend a favor
daily.description: Casually asking a close friend.
daily.example: Is it OK if I call you later?

work.title: Talking with a coworker
work.description: Softly suggesting something to a coworker you're close to.
work.example: Do you think this document can be done by tomorrow?

work.title: Thinking over a plan
work.description: Talking to yourself while preparing a proposal.
work.example: I wonder if they'll understand this explanation.

etymology: It combines the question particle 「か」 and the exclamatory particle 「な」. It mixes a question with your own feelings, which gives it a talking-to-yourself flavor.
formation: Made of the question particle 「か」 + the exclamatory sentence-final particle 「な」. 「か」 raises a question, and 「な」 is originally an exclamation said to yourself (「いい天気だな」). A question followed by a self-directed exclamation becomes “…? I wonder”, which doesn't directly ask the other person to answer, so it expresses wondering or puzzling to yourself. Because it doesn't demand an answer, saying 「手伝ってくれるかな」 to someone becomes a soft request that leaves room to refuse. With the negative 「ないかな」, “won't it …?” turns into the wish “if only …”. Stretched out to 「かなあ」, the tone of uncertainty or emotion gets stronger.

similar.title: 〜かしら
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both express wondering to yourself or a soft question. 「かしら」 is traditionally feminine and sounds gentle and a bit old-fashioned; 「かな」 is commonly used by both men and women.

similar.title: 〜のだろうか
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both are self-questions, “I wonder …?”. 「〜のだろうか」 leans toward writing and sounds serious, used in texts or deep thinking; 「〜かな」 is relaxed spoken language.

similar.title: 〜ないかな (wish)
similar.explanation: Same origin: adding the negative 「ない」 before 「かな」 turns it into a wish, “if only …”: 「早く来ないかな」. Plain 「かな」 just wonders “will it …?”.

similar.title: 〜なあ・〜な (exclamation)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the 「な」 in 「かな」 is the exclamatory 「な」. 「きれいだなあ」 is just an exclamation; adding the question 「か」 to make 「かなあ」 adds a sense of uncertainty.

meaning: A soft sentence ending used mainly by women, for wondering to oneself or for asking and requesting gently.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form, or na-adjective stem / noun + かしら

senses.label: Wondering
senses.meaning: The speaker isn't sure about something and wonders aloud, like “I wonder ...”. The tone is soft and feminine.
senses.connection: Plain form + かしら; often with question words like 「どう」, 「誰」, 「どこ」
examples: I wonder who that person is.
I wonder if this outfit suits me.
I wonder how many minutes it takes to the station.

senses.label: Soft request / hope
senses.meaning: 「〜てくれないかしら」 and 「〜ないかしら」 make soft requests or hopes, like “Would you mind ...?” or “I wish ...”.
senses.connection: 〜てくれないかしら／〜てもらえるかしら／verb nai-form + かしら
examples: Would you mind opening the window a little?
I wish the rain would stop soon.

notes: 「かしら」 has a clearly feminine flavor. If a man uses it in daily life, it can sound affected or like he's imitating a woman. Learners just need to understand it; men usually say 「〜かな」.
Even women don't use 「かしら」 with bosses or clients: ✕「資料を送っていただけないかしら」→ ○「資料を送っていただけないでしょうか」.
「〜ないかしら」 usually expresses a wish, not a negative guess: 「早く春にならないかしら」 means “I wish spring would come soon”.
Attach 「かしら」 directly after nouns and na-adjectives, without 「だ」: ✕「本当だかしら」→ ○「本当かしら」.

daily.title: Mom preparing dinner
daily.description: A mother talks to herself while cooking.
daily.example: I wonder what I should make tonight.

daily.title: Seen in a novel
daily.description: A female character's inner thoughts in a novel.
daily.example: I wonder if he'll really come.

work.title: A female boss asking politely
work.description: An older female boss politely gives a task to a subordinate.
work.example: Could you make copies of this document for me?

etymology: It is generally thought to come from 「〜か知らん」 (“I don't know if ...”): 「か」 + 「知らぬ（知らん）」, the old negative of 「知る」. It later changed to 「かしらん→かしら」 and became popular in women's speech from the Edo period.
formation: It is generally thought to come from 「か知らん」: the question particle 「か」 + 「知らん（知らぬ）」, an old negative form of 「知る」. Literally it means “whether …, I don't know”. It was shortened to 「かしらん」 and then to 「かしら」. “I don't know whether …” is exactly the meaning of wondering to yourself. When said to others, as in 「〜てくれないかしら」, it makes a roundabout request, “I wonder if you could …”, instead of a direct demand, so the tone is soft. The 「かしらん」 you occasionally hear is the older form that still keeps a trace of 「知らん」.

similar.title: 〜かな
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both express wondering to yourself or a soft question. 「かな」 is used by men and women and is fairly casual; 「かしら」 leans feminine and sounds refined and gentle, and young people today use it less.

similar.title: 〜のだろうか
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both are self-questions, “I wonder …?”. 「〜のだろうか」 is a neutral written expression; 「かしら」 is feminine speech.

similar.title: 〜でしょう (guess / confirmation)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜でしょうか」 is a polite-style question that can be used with superiors and clients; 「かしら」 is plain-style speech used only with people close to you or when talking to yourself.

meaning: Friendly casual question endings used by men or older people: 「かい」 for yes-no questions, 「だい」 for questions with a question word.
connection: Yes-no question: plain form / noun + かい; with a question word: question word ... + (の・ん) だい

senses.label: Yes-no question
senses.meaning: Asks a yes-or-no question, like “...?”. The tone is warm and relaxed, often from older people to younger ones, or from men to people they know.
senses.connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form + かい／〜のかい; noun / na-adjective + かい
examples: Have you finished your homework already?
Want to come along?
How are you doing?

senses.label: Question-word question
senses.meaning: With a question word like 「何」, 「どこ」, 「誰」, or 「どう」, use 「だい」, like “what / where ...?”. Often as 「〜んだい／〜のだい」.
senses.connection: Question word ... + だい／〜んだい
examples: What's the matter?
What's your name?
When are you coming back?

notes: Use 「だい」 with a question word and 「かい」 without one: ○「何だい？」 ○「本当かい？」 ✕「何かい？」 ✕「本当だい？」.
This is how elders talk to younger people or superiors talk to subordinates. Using it with a boss, client or elder sounds condescending and very rude.
With falling intonation it becomes a retort or irony: 「そんなことあるかい」 means “As if that could happen!”, the exact opposite of asking.
Women and young people rarely use it in daily life. If learners imitate it, they sound old-fashioned or like they're acting; just understanding it is enough.

daily.title: Grandpa asks his grandson
daily.description: A grandfather kindly asks how his grandson is doing.
daily.example: Is school fun?

daily.title: A father checks on his child
daily.description: Seeing his child looking down, the father asks.
daily.example: Did something happen?

daily.title: Seen in a novel
daily.description: A male character's line in a novel.
daily.example: Where are you going?

work.title: An older boss to a junior
work.description: A senior male boss casually asks a young subordinate.
work.example: Is that work of yours finished already?

etymology: 「かい」 is generally thought to be the question particle 「か」 + the exclamatory particle 「い」. 「だい」 is the copula 「だ」 + 「い」. Adding 「い」 makes the tone softer and friendlier.
formation: Generally thought to be made of “question or assertion” + the sentence-final particle 「い」: 「か」 + 「い」 → 「かい」, 「だ」 + 「い」 → 「だい」. 「い」 is an old sentence-final particle that adds a friendly feel of addressing the other person. A yes-no question needs 「か」 to mark it as a question, so it becomes 「かい」. In a sentence with a question word, the question word already carries the question, so the end only needs the assertion 「だ」 (「何だ」), and adding 「い」 gives 「何だい」. So the rule “だい with a question word, かい without one” comes directly from how the forms are built.

similar.title: 〜か (question)
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「かい」 is simply 「か」 + 「い」. Ending a plain-form sentence with just 「か」 (「行くか？」) sounds blunt; 「行くかい？」 sounds friendly.

similar.title: 〜の？ (casual question)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both are plain-style spoken questions. 「〜の？」 is used by everyone, young and old, and is the most common; 「〜かい・〜だい」 has a masculine or elderly feel and is less common in modern speech.

similar.title: 〜ものか・〜もんか
similar.explanation: Similar meaning (rhetorical use): a 「〜かい」 with falling intonation (「行くかい！」) and 「〜ものか」 both mean “no way I'd …”. 「ものか」 is stronger and clearer, a dedicated rhetorical pattern.

meaning: A casual plain-form question ending that shows concern or curiosity, wanting to know the situation. It sounds softer than 「か」.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form, or noun / na-adjective + なの + ？ (rising intonation)

senses.label: Asking out of concern
senses.meaning: Seeing how the other person looks, you want to know what's behind it, like “What's wrong?” or “Are you ...?”. It shows concern.
senses.connection: Plain form + の？; noun / na-adjective + なの？
examples: What's wrong?
You look pale. Are you OK?
Does something hurt?

senses.label: Asking for an explanation
senses.meaning: Asks the other person to explain a reason or situation. Often with 「なんで」 or 「どうして」, and sometimes sounds like blame.
senses.connection: なんで／どうして + plain form + の？
examples: Why didn't you come yesterday?
What are you laughing at?

senses.label: Surprised confirmation
senses.meaning: Shows surprise at something unexpected and checks with the other person, like “Really ...?”.
senses.connection: え、／もう + plain form + の？
examples: What, you're leaving already?
Did you really make it all by yourself?

notes: After nouns and na-adjectives, add 「な」: ✕「学生の？」→ ○「学生なの？」; ✕「静かの？」→ ○「静かなの？」.
Use 「〜の？」 only with friends, family and younger people. Saying 「どこに行くの？」 to a boss or client sounds like talking to a child and is very rude; say 「どちらへ行かれるんですか」.
「どうして〜の？」 and 「なんで〜の？」 easily sound blaming or accusing: 「どうして来なかったの？」. If you're just concerned, you can say 「何かあったの？」.
The end must have rising intonation. A falling 「〜の。」 is an explanation in a feminine or childlike tone (「明日、行くの。」 = I'm going tomorrow), not a question.

daily.title: A friend is feeling down
daily.description: Seeing a friend low on energy, you ask with concern.
daily.example: You don't look well. Did something happen?

daily.title: A family member suddenly goes out
daily.description: A family member gets dressed to go out late at night.
daily.example: Where are you going at this hour?

daily.title: A friend is moving
daily.description: Hearing a friend is moving, you check in surprise.
daily.example: What, you're moving?

work.title: Chatting with a coworker
work.description: Chatting with a coworker you're close to during lunch.
work.example: Did you bring a boxed lunch today?

etymology: It comes from the explanatory 「〜のだ／〜のです」: drop 「ですか」 from 「〜のですか」 and 「の」 remains, with rising intonation marking the question. That's why it keeps the sense of asking about the background.
formation: Comes from the 「の」 of the explanatory 「〜のだ」. 「の」 was originally a formal noun that packages a sentence as “this matter, this situation”, so 「〜のですか」 means “is that how it is?”. In speech, 「ですか」 is dropped, leaving only 「の」 with rising intonation to make a question. That's why 「〜の？」 asks not just about the fact itself but about “what's behind it”, carrying concern or curiosity, and sometimes a pressing tone. Adding 「な」 after nouns and na-adjectives, as in 「なのだ」, also follows from this origin.

similar.title: 〜んです・〜のです
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜の？」 is the plain, spoken form of 「〜んですか」, and both carry the nuance of asking about the situation behind something. With people you don't know well or superiors, use 「〜んですか」.

similar.title: 〜か (question)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: plain-style 「行くか？」 sounds blunt and is mostly used by men; 「行くの？」 is soft and natural, used by both men and women.

similar.title: 〜かい・〜だい
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both are plain-style spoken questions. 「〜かい・〜だい」 has an elderly or masculine feel; 「〜の？」 is the most widely used.

meaning: Uses a negative question to invite or suggest casually, like “Why don't we ...?” or “Do you want to ...?”.
connection: Verb nai-form + ？ (rising intonation); men also say 「〜ないか」

senses.label: Invitation
senses.meaning: Invites someone to do something together, like “Do you want to ...?” or “Why don't we ...?”. The negative form leaves room for the other person to say no, so it sounds considerate.
senses.connection: (一緒に) + verb nai-form + ？; 「〜に行かない？」 and 「〜てみない？」 are very common
examples: Do you want to see a movie together this Sunday?
A new café opened in front of the station. Want to go?
Why don't we go home together?

senses.label: Suggestion
senses.meaning: Suggests doing something, sounding like a discussion, like “How about ...?” or “Shall we ...?”.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ？; often with 「ちょっと」 or 「そろそろ」
examples: Why don't we take a short break?
Shouldn't we get going soon?

notes: Use 「〜ない？」 only with friends and family. To invite a boss or client, say 「〜ませんか」, or more politely 「ご一緒にいかがですか」.
The invitation depends on rising intonation: 「行かない？」 (rising) means “Want to go?”, while 「行かない。」 (falling) means “I'm not going”, the complete opposite. In writing, add 「？」.
Negative questions with adjectives, such as 「面白くない？」 and 「いいじゃない？」, mean “don't you think …?”, not an invitation.
Answering an invitation with a flat 「行かない」 is blunt and hurtful. To decline, people usually say 「ごめん、今日はちょっと…」, trailing off to soften it.

daily.title: Inviting a friend to eat
daily.description: Inviting a classmate to eat together after class.
daily.example: Want to have lunch together?

daily.title: A weekend outing
daily.description: Discussing weekend plans with your partner.
daily.example: Want to go to the beach this weekend?

daily.title: Suggesting a break
daily.description: Suggesting a break while studying together.
daily.example: We're tired, huh. How about some tea?

work.title: Inviting a coworker from your year
work.description: Inviting a coworker who joined the company with you, after work.
work.example: Want to go for a drink after work?

etymology: 「ない」 is the negative auxiliary. Inviting with “won't you ...?” is a polite strategy that leaves the decision to the other person, just like the polite 「〜ませんか」.
formation: Made of the verb's nai-form (negative) + rising question intonation. Literally it's “won't you …?”; on the surface it asks whether the other person will “not do” it, but in fact it hands them the decision whether to do it: answering 「うん、行く」 or 「ごめん」 is equally comfortable. At the same time, a negative question implies “I think going would be nice”, so it sounds more like a suggestion or invitation than the positive question 「行く？」. The polite 「〜ませんか」 uses exactly the same structure.

similar.title: 〜ませんか
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜ませんか」 is the polite version of the same “negative-question invitation” and can be used with people you don't know well or superiors; 「〜ない？」 is plain style, only for people close to you.

similar.title: 〜(よ)う (volitional form)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: plain 「行こう」 is a direct call, “let's go”, assuming the other person will agree; 「行かない？」 first asks what they want, which is softer and makes it easy for them to say no.

similar.title: 〜ましょう
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜ましょう」 is the polite “let's do it”, often used for something already agreed on. When you haven't confirmed the other person's wishes yet, 「〜ませんか」 / 「〜ない？」 is more appropriate.

meaning: First explain your situation with 「〜んですが／〜んですけど」, then make a request, ask a question, or ask for help. A very common way to open a conversation.
connection: Plain form (noun / na-adjective + な) + んですが／んですけど (casual: んだけど)

senses.label: Leading into a request
senses.meaning: Explains the situation first, then makes a request, like “The thing is ..., could you ...?”. Softer than asking directly.
senses.connection: 〜んですが + 〜ていただけませんか／〜てもらえませんか
examples: I wrote a composition in Japanese. Could you take a look at it?
I forgot my pen. Could I borrow yours?

senses.label: Leading into a question
senses.meaning: Explains your situation first, then asks how to do something or for an opinion, like “I'd like to ..., but how ...?”. Often followed by 「どうすればいいですか」.
senses.connection: 〜たいんですが／〜んですが + どうすればいいですか／どこですか
examples: I'd like to go to city hall. How do I get there?
My computer won't work. What should I do?

senses.label: Leaving it unsaid
senses.meaning: Only states the situation and leaves out the request, letting the listener understand. Very soft. Often ends with 「…」.
senses.connection: 〜んですが…／〜んですけど… (second half left out)
examples: Um, I'm not feeling very well...
This seat isn't free, actually...

notes: Dropping 「ん」 at the start sounds stiff: ✕「予約したいですが」→ ○「予約したいんですが」. 「ん」 brings in the explanatory tone of “here's my situation”, which sets up the request.
The 「が・けど」 here isn't “but”, and nothing contrasting needs to follow. In a shop or on the phone, jumping straight to 「〜してください」 sounds abrupt; opening with 「すみません、〜んですが」 is more polite.
After nouns and na-adjectives, add 「な」: ✕「学生んですが」→ ○「学生なんですが」; ✕「暇んですけど」→ ○「暇なんですけど」.
In speech, trailing off with 「〜んですが…」 is polite and the other person will pick it up. But in emails and documents, write the request out in full; don't stop at 「…」.

daily.title: Asking a shop clerk
daily.description: A customer explains what they need.
daily.example: I'm looking for this shirt in a larger size.

daily.title: Asking for directions
daily.description: Telling a passerby where you want to go.
daily.example: I want to get to the station. Is this the right way?

work.title: Calling to ask for someone
work.description: Opening a phone call to a client's company.
work.example: I'd like to speak with Mr. Tanaka in the sales department.

work.title: Asking your boss for time off
work.description: Explaining the situation first, then asking for approval.
work.example: I have a family matter next week. Would it be all right to take a day off?

etymology: It is the explanatory 「〜んです」 + the conjunctive particle 「が／けど」. 「が」 originally meant “but”, but here it has weakened into a way of leading into what follows.
formation: Made of the explanatory 「〜んです」 + the conjunctive particle 「が・けど」. 「〜んです」 first lays out “this is my situation”. 「が」 is originally a conjunctive particle linking two clauses; here it shows no contrast but signals “I'm not finished, there's more”, steering the conversation toward a request or question. Because the listener understands from 「〜んですが」 alone that “this person wants something”, they will respond even if the second half is left out. This structure, stating your situation first without spelling out the request, is a typical way of opening a conversation politely in Japanese.

similar.title: 〜んです・〜のです
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜んです」 by itself explains a situation; adding 「が・けど」 turns it into a preface, followed by a request or question.

similar.title: 〜が (contrast)
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use the conjunctive particle 「が」. Ordinary 「〜が」 contrasts two opposing ideas (「高いが、おいしい」); the 「が」 in 「〜んですが」 doesn't contrast anything, it just opens the topic and leads into what follows.

similar.title: 〜けど・〜けれども
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜んですけど」 is the spoken version of 「〜んですが」, with the same meaning but more relaxed. In formal situations and with clients, 「〜んですが」 or 「〜のですが」 is more common.

meaning: Moves the information you want to stress to the end, before 「〜だ」, as the focus. The known part comes first with 「〜のは」. Like the English “It's ... that ...” or “What ... is ...”.
connection: Plain form (noun / na-adjective + な) + のは + focused part + だ／です

senses.label: Focusing on a person, thing, time, or place
senses.meaning: Takes one part of the sentence (who, what, when, where) and puts it at the end for emphasis, like “It was ... who/that ...”.
senses.connection: 〜のは + noun + だ／です
examples: Osaka is where I was born.
It was three years ago that I first met him.
It was my younger sister who painted this picture.

senses.label: Focusing on a reason or purpose
senses.meaning: Emphasizes a reason or purpose, often as 「〜のは〜からだ」 or 「〜のは〜ためだ」, like “The reason ... is that ...”.
senses.connection: 〜のは + 〜から／〜ため + だ／です
examples: The reason I was late is that I overslept.
I came to Japan to study Japanese.

senses.label: Stating the key point
senses.meaning: Introduces the most important point with 「大切なのは」, 「問題なのは」, and so on, like “What's important is ...”.
senses.connection: Na-adjective / noun + なのは + 〜ことだ／noun + だ
examples: What's important is to keep at it every day.
The problem is that there's no time.

notes: The subject of the clause before 「のは」 takes 「が」: ✕「私は生まれたのは大阪だ」→ ○「私が生まれたのは大阪だ」.
Drop 「が・を」 from the focused part: ✕「買ったのはこの本をです」→ ○「買ったのはこの本です」. Particles like 「から・で・まで」 can stay: 「来たのは東京からです」.
To emphasize a reason, use 「からだ」, not 「ので」: ✕「遅れたのは雨が降ったのでだ」→ ○「遅れたのは雨が降ったからだ」.
Saying 「間違えたのはあなたです」 to someone's face pins the blame directly on them and sounds very harsh. At work, point out problems indirectly, e.g. 「ここが少し違っているようです」.

daily.title: Correcting a misunderstanding
daily.description: A friend thinks you made the cake; you explain who really did.
daily.example: It was my mom who made this.

daily.title: Explaining why you're late
daily.description: Telling a friend the reason.
daily.example: The reason I'm late is that the train stopped.

work.title: Summing up a meeting
work.description: Stressing the most important point before the meeting ends.
work.example: What matters most is listening to our customers.

work.title: Reporting the cause of a problem
work.description: Explaining the cause of a failure to your boss.
work.example: The error occurred because the data was out of date.

etymology: It is made of the nominalizer 「の」 + the topic particle 「は」, with the copula 「だ」 at the end. The known part is wrapped up as the topic and the focus comes last, much like English “What I need is ...” sentences.
formation: Made of nominalizing 「の」 + the topic particle 「は」 + the sentence-final assertion 「だ」. First 「の」 packages the part both sides already know into a single matter, and 「は」 raises it as the topic; the new information you want to stress goes at the end, asserted with 「だ」. In Japanese, the end of the sentence is the focus position, so moving an element before 「だ」 makes it stand out, like the English cleft sentence “It was … that …”. Also, because the first part is a clause wrapped in 「の」, its subject takes 「が」, not 「は」.

similar.title: 〜のは〜からだ
similar.explanation: Same origin: the set form of this pattern for emphasizing a reason. State the result first with 「〜のは」, then give the reason at the end with 「〜からだ」: 「遅れたのは寝坊したからだ」.

similar.title: 〜の (nominalizer)
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜のは」 + adjective (「話すのは楽しい」) is a nominalized subject; 「〜のは」 + noun + 「だ」 puts the focus on the noun and is an emphatic sentence.

similar.title: 〜こそ
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both highlight one part. 「こそ」 attaches directly to the word you want to stress (「この本こそ読みたい」) and is stronger, meaning “this very …, precisely”; 「〜のは〜だ」 highlights by moving the information to the end of the sentence.
